Issued at 315 PM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

Today was yet another unseasonably warm mid-October day across 
Chicagoland. The weak cold front that moved into the area
earlier this morning has since stalled out south of I-80 which 
has resulted in a notable temperature gradient from northwest 
(mid 70s) to southeast (upper 80s). A couple of areas of
altocumulus (one overhead and another crossing the Mississippi 
River) associated with narrow pockets of mid-level moisture have
managed to produce isolated showers/sprinkles. Think this 
activity will remain fairly isolated through the early evening 
hours but can't rule out a few showers or a rumble of thunder.

Focus continues to be on the potential for scattered showers 
and thunderstorms later this evening through the overnight 
hours. Model guidance has remained varied on the timing and 
placement of the greatest coverage of showers, likely owing to 
differences in the handling of the timing and placement of 
subtle vort lobes and areas of drier air between plumes of 
increasing moisture. This is especially evident in regional
satellite and radar imagery showing large gaps between ongoing 
convection and areas of ACCAS. Nevertheless, the presence of 
sufficient synoptic forcing within the right entrance of the 
upper jet and moist air lifting atop a stalled surface boundary 
support an eventual increase in shower and storm coverage
overnight, and potentially developing as early as 8-9 PM if 
some of the earlier hi-res guidance verifies. Overall weaker
mid-level lapse rates should limit storm strength overall even 
in the presence of favorable shear for hail. Thus, will continue
to message the potential for small hail with the strongest 
storms with the severe potential remaining mainly southwest of 
the area.

The threat of lightning quickly wanes toward daybreak Wednesday
with shower coverage beginning to focus south of the area. 
However, residual low to mid-level moisture in the presence of 
weak ascent may support lingering light rain or drizzle through 
part of the morning. Expanding high pressure across the western
Great Lakes will eventually shift this south of the area toward
midday, with dry conditions forecast through the remainder of 
the afternoon and evening hours. Persistent north to 
northeasterly winds will bring temperatures back to more 
seasonable levels with highs in the 60s for most of the area and
lower 70s well south of I-80.

This brief break in precipitation will be fairly short lived as
energy ejecting off the Rockies will phase with a wave diving
southeast toward the Upper Midwest late Wednesday night into
Thursday. An associated developing low pressure system will 
move across the area bringing widespread showers and a chance of
thunderstorms on Thursday.

Petr


Friday Onward: 

As the surface low pulls away (and deepens toward 990 mb in 
southern Ontario), the arrival of a strong (nearly 1040 mb) 
surface high pressure system into the central Plains will set 
the stage for an impressive pressure gradient across the Great 
Lakes. Accordingly, do expect a windy day on Friday with early 
BUFKIT mixing profiles supporting frequent gusts of 30 to 40 
mph. Such strong winds will facilitate aggressive low-level cold
air advection in the wake of the cyclone with mean 850mb 
temperatures plummeting 10 to 15 degrees C in 24 hours (to near 
or below 0C). Taken together, Friday will feel every bit like 
October with highs in the 50s, blustery northwest winds, and 
showers of leaves (not water) flying through the air. With that
said, a notable temperature difference between Lake Michigan 
water and the fall airmass will support lake effect rain showers
mainly east of Gary. 

There remains ensemble agreement that the surface high will 
slide directly over the Great Lakes Friday night into Saturday 
morning setting the stage for ideal radiational cooling and the
coldest night of the autumn season so far. Assuming no major 
changes in forecast guidance, would expect areas of frost and 
even locally freezing temperatures across the region right in 
line with climatology (the first freezing temperatures away from
Lake Michigan typically occur in the October 11 to 20 
timeframe). 

Thereafter, ensemble guidance advertises the surface high 
stalling over the Atlantic Seaboard and the northward-shift of 
the dominant upper-level jet into Canada supporting gradually 
rising temperatures into next week. 

Borchardt
